# Machine tools (planer, shaper, milling machine) (`machine_tools`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: needs lathe_screw_cutting, precision_measurement; helped by high_pressure_steam, crucible_steel, belt_drive
- Core idea: Machine tools are the machines that make machine parts, and their rule is that the machine, not the hand, guides the cutter. The lathe makes round surfaces. The planer makes flat ones: the work is bolted to a table that slides to and fro on straight ways under a fixed single-point tool, which is stepped sideways after each stroke (in the smaller shaper the tool moves instead). The milling machine feeds the work past a rotating cutter with many teeth and produces flats, grooves and shaped profiles, identical every time; it is the key to making gun and sewing-machine parts alike. Drilling, boring and later grinding machines complete the set. Each generation of machine tools is built on the last and can be more accurate than it, because straightness and flatness come from scraping to a reference plate.
- Pitfalls:
  - Light frames: a machine tool must be many times stiffer than the cut seems to need, or it chatters
  - Expecting hand filing and chiselling to give flat surfaces for steam-tight joints at any reasonable cost
  - Carbon steel cutters run too fast lose their hardness; before 1900 cutting speeds are a few metres a minute
  - Crediting single inventors: planer and miller appeared in several workshops at once
- History: europe: 1751 – Nicolas Focq's planing machine in France; c. 1802–1807 Bramah, and Brunel and Maudslay's block-making machines at Portsmouth; c. 1817 Richard Roberts's planer (also Fox, Murray, Clement); 1836 Nasmyth's shaper; 1839–1842 steam hammer; 1830s–1850s Whitworth's standardised tools; americas: c. 1816–1820 – milling machines in the federal armouries and their contractors (Simeon North, John Hall; credit to Eli Whitney is doubtful); 1840s–1850s turret lathe; 1862 Brown and Sharpe universal milling machine; 1900 Taylor and White's high-speed steel
- Read:
  - Joseph Wickham Roe, English and American Tool Builders (1916)
  - L. T. C. Rolt, Tools for the Job: A Short History of Machine Tools (1965)
